subject: zoology_2
question_text: What are the major transport mechanisms for CO₂? Explain.

mark_split.label: The three ways with their shares

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book p.30, SAQ 16. insider_note: The three percentages are what separate a full answer from a half one. Write them beside each route.

page_header: Breathing and Exchange of Gases · 4 marks

steps.label: Three ways
steps.why: The percentages are the answer: they show at once that almost all the carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate, not as gas.
common_mistakes: Writing that CO₂ is carried mainly by haemoglobin. Only about a quarter is.
Giving no percentages. The three shares carry this mark.
steps.margin_note: Open with the list, then take the three in order.
lines: Carbon dioxide is carried to the lungs in
three ways:
1. About 7% as carbonic acid.
2. About 20 to 25% as carbamino compound.
3. About 70% as bicarbonates.

steps.label: As carbonic acid
steps.why: A small part of the gas simply dissolves and reacts with the water of the plasma, needing no carrier at all.
common_mistakes: Giving this route the largest share. It is the smallest.
Forgetting that the reaction runs backwards at the lungs.
steps.memory_tip: The smallest share travels as plain acid in the plasma.
steps.margin_note: Two lines. Say what forms and where it breaks up.
lines: About 7% of CO₂ combines with water to
form carbonic acid.
It is carried to the lungs, where it splits
again into water and CO₂.

steps.label: As carbamino compound
steps.why: Carbon dioxide binds to the amino groups of the globin chains, not to the iron, which is why it does not compete with oxygen.
common_mistakes: Writing that CO₂ binds to the iron of haem. It binds to the amino group.
Calling the reaction irreversible. It is reversible.
steps.memory_tip: Carbamino means it clips onto the amino group of globin.
steps.margin_note: The equation line is worth writing out.
lines: About 20 to 25% of CO₂ combines with the
free amino group of haemoglobin and forms
carbamino haemoglobin.
It is a reversible reaction.

steps.label: As bicarbonate
steps.why: Carbonic anhydrase inside the red cell speeds the reaction thousands of times, which is what makes this the main route.
common_mistakes: Leaving out carbonic anhydrase. Without the enzyme the route is too slow.
Writing that the reaction goes the same way at the lungs. It reverses there.
steps.memory_tip: Enzyme in the red cell, bicarbonate out into the plasma.
steps.margin_note: End with the reversal at the alveoli.
lines: About 70% of CO₂ combines with water to
form H₂CO₃ in the presence of carbonic
anhydrase inside the red blood cells.
The carbonic acid dissociates into HCO₃⁻
and H⁺.
At the alveoli, where pCO₂ is low, the
reaction runs the opposite way and gives
back CO₂ and water.
